summary: This informational RFC discusses problems that arise when the IPv6 address of a Dual-Stack Lite B4 element changes, since the carrier-side NAT ties its state to that address. It sketches recommendations for keeping connections working in this case.

eli5.summary: If a house changes its address, the mailman can no longer find the old letters. This gives ideas for keeping the mail flowing when addresses change.

subtitle: Keeping connections stable when a customer's IPv6 address changes

tldr.problem: In Dual-Stack Lite, when a B4 element (customer gateway) gets a new IPv6 address, the carrier-side NAT can no longer track its existing connections.
tldr.mechanism: Instead of tracking by the B4's exact IPv6 address, track by the IPv6 prefix delegated to the customer. Use a configurable mask (typically /56) to derive the prefix from any B4 address.
tldr.outcome: Connections remain stable even when customer equipment reboots or the B4 gets a new IPv6 address, avoiding service disruption and resource waste.

today: RFC 7785 is an Informational RFC offering practical guidance for DS-Lite deployments. It has not been obsoleted and remains a recommended practice for carrier-grade NAT systems that use DS-Lite.

sections.title: Understanding Dual-Stack Lite and the B4
sections.content:
Dual-Stack Lite (DS-Lite) is a way for Internet providers to deliver IPv4 services over an IPv6 network when IPv4 addresses are scarce. A B4 element is the customer's device (usually built into a residential gateway) that creates a tunnel from IPv4 traffic to the provider's carrier-side NAT, called an AFTR (Address Family Transition Router).

The B4 uses an IPv6 address to identify itself on the provider's network. When the B4's IPv6 address changes—because the customer reboots their equipment, the lease expires, or privacy extensions are in use—the AFTR's NAT tables can become invalid, because they are keyed to the old IPv6 address.
sections.eli5: A B4 is like your home address on the IPv6 network. When it changes, the post office loses track of where to send your mail.

sections.title: The Problem When Addresses Change
sections.content:
The AFTR maintains connection state keyed by the B4's IPv6 address. This state includes mappings for outbound traffic (which external IPv4 address and port to use), resource limits per customer, and PCP (Port Control Protocol) mappings that servers behind the B4 have created. When the B4's IPv6 address changes, all this state becomes orphaned.

A misbehaving customer could also deliberately change their B4's IPv6 address repeatedly to evade resource limits and exhaust AFTR capacity—a denial-of-service risk. Even without malice, stale mappings consume memory and can break existing connections, degrading quality of service for the customer.
sections.eli5: Old phone numbers for customers stay in the system and clog it up. A bad actor could keep changing their number to get more phone lines.

sections.title: The Subscriber-Mask Solution
sections.content:
Instead of keying connection state to the individual B4 address, the AFTR should key it to the IPv6 prefix delegated to the customer. The RFC introduces a subscriber-mask—a configurable bit length, defaulting to 56—that the AFTR applies to the B4's source IPv6 address to derive the customer's prefix.

For example, if the customer is assigned the prefix 2001:db8:100:100::/56 and the B4 has address 2001:db8:100:100::1, applying a /56 mask yields 2001:db8:100:100::/56. Even if the B4 later uses 2001:db8:100:100::2, the mask still yields the same prefix, so the AFTR can reuse the same connection state.
sections.eli5: Remember which neighborhood the house is in, not the exact house number. Even if the house number changes, you know it's the same customer.

sections.title: Recommendations for Implementation
sections.content:
The RFC makes six key recommendations. First, the AFTR should limit to one active DS-Lite softwire per subscriber to prevent resource exhaustion. Second, resource contexts (connection limits, NAT pool resources, PCP mappings) should be per-prefix, not per-tunnel.

Third, when a new B4 address from the same prefix arrives, the AFTR should migrate existing state to it and forward future return traffic to the new address. Fourth, the B4 should send PCP ANNOUNCE messages when the prefix changes so that servers behind it can update their dynamic DNS. Fifth, the provider should assign stable IPv6 prefixes; and sixth, if a prefix must be reassigned to a different customer, it should wait until all state from the old customer is cleared.
sections.eli5: Let one customer have one tunnel. Keep their records by neighborhood. When they move within the neighborhood, update the address but keep their connection. Tell servers about the move. Try not to reassign neighborhoods. If you must, clean up the old records first.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The recommendations defend against denial-of-service attacks in which a customer repeatedly changes their B4 address to exhaust AFTR resources. Rate-limiting—setting a 30-minute floor between address changes from the same prefix—mitigates this threat. A misbehaving customer can be identified and blacklisted by their prefix.

The RFC does not introduce new privacy concerns beyond those in DS-Lite itself. Because the subscriber-mask depends on a delegated IPv6 prefix, even if privacy extensions generate multiple B4 addresses, the customer can be tracked within a single prefix, but not across renumbering events. The recommendations actually help protect privacy by ensuring old state is cleared promptly when prefixes change.
sections.eli5: Rate-limiting stops someone from rapidly changing their address to grab more resources. Clearing old records prevents someone else's data from leaking to a new customer.
